newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's mobile telephone firms bemoan losses.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's mobile telephone firms bemoan losses.

text.p: Pakistan's cellular telephone industry has told the government that it is losing money due to low consumer tariffs, high taxes and a 17-month-old suspension of mobile telephone services in Karachi, its biggest market.
A document outlining the industry's woes was presented to the government recently on behalf of the chief executives of the three mobile telephone companies operating in Pakistan.
The paper, obtained by Reuters, said the firms had suffered combined losses of 2.2 billion rupees ($54.7 million) and had an average negative return on capital employed of 36 percent.
"Tariffs in Pakistan are the lowest in Asia and the industry's appeal for a revision has been outstanding since December 1994," the document said.

"The industry has paid 1.8 billion rupees to the government in taxes, duties and royalties and further 2.7 billion rupees has been generated for PTCL (Pakistan Telecommunication Company Ltd) in call revenue."
It said the mobile telephone industry had invested 6.3 billion rupees in infrastructure in the past six years, but conditions made further investment a daunting prospect.
"Infrastructure is taxed so highly that operators are restrained from further development, customers are taxed so highly on usage that they either won't buy or are ceasing usage," the document said.

It said that imposition in June of a 40 percent central excise duty on customer usage and 10 percent advanced income tax were already constraining demand and the government and PTCL would be receiving less revenue by October 1997.

The three cellular telephone companies are Pakistan Mobile Telecommunications, a joint venture of U.S.-based Motorola Inc and local Saif Telecom; Pakcom Ltd, a subsidiary of Luxembourg's Millicom; and Paktel Ltd, a subsidiary of Cable and Wireless Plc.
The document said loss of revenue from Karachi and Hyderabad, where the government suspended services on security grounds in July 1995, was a major problem for the industry.
The caretaker government decided last month to restore the services but has asked the telephone companies to sign a waiver foregoing their right to demand compensation for the ban.

"This is a condition which none of the three operators has agreed to," one telephone company executive said. "If this and some other conditions are not withdrawn by the government, we are better off without a service in Karachi," he said.
Government officials were not immediately available for comment.

Javaid Feroze, a director at Pakistan's Telecard Ltd, said his firm would not withdraw a claim it filed on July 24 for 2.2 billion rupees in damages from the government for business it says it lost as a result of the suspension of its pay-card telephone service in Karachi last year.

Throughout the suspension, the cellular telephone operators, as well as a pager company and three telephone booth card companies, have stayed ready to resume business in Karachi, which accounts for about 40 percent of their Pakistan revenue.
